transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-06 15:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Ellen (Redwood AE), Rajat (Redwood SE), Maya (Product), Jonas (Solutions) — Aisha (CTO), Tom (Lead ML Eng), Priya (Head of Security), Marcus (SRE), Devon (PM)

Summary (auto): Ellen opened with goals — show JSON mode, tool safety, and how a pilot would look. Customer emphasized security/compliance and predictable latency during spikes.

[00:00] Ellen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick round of intros then i'll hand to rajat for a short runthrough of the json mode demo — hi aisha, tom, priya, marcus — great to see you
[00:18] Aisha: hey, thanks. we're most interested in seeing the guardrails — Priya cares a lot about the auditability piece — and Marcus will want to stress test the canary fallback behavior
[00:28] Rajat: cool, i'll share my screen in a sec. Goal: show contract-first schemas, function binding, and a safe execution path with a fallback to a cheaper model variant. We'll also touch on KV cache and batching — note, we call it K V cache sometimes in our docs, sorry the transcript hates that word
[00:50] Tom: quick Q before you jump in — what's the latency delta when we enforce strict schema checks at generation time? like, do we pay significant p99 penalty?
[01:05] Rajat: good question — typically negligible at token-time with our runtime; the schema verification happens in the Aurora layer — that's post-decode validation plus a small parse/repair step. In our internal benchmarks enforcing schema with typed responses increased tail by ~5-15ms on average but it depends on model and sequence length
[01:30] Priya: and how is the verification logged? we need per-request audit logs, and we have to show the pre/post payloads for regulatory reasons
[01:44] Ellen: yep, we export audit trails per request, with optional redaction. We integrate with customer KMS for encryption at rest, and we can send logs to your SIEM or to a dedicated S3 bucket in your VPC. Security pack link: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2.pdf
[02:05] Devon: are there any known gotchas with air gap or on-prem? our infra team may request an air-gap image later
[02:14] Rajat: on-prem is doable — we have an on-prem package, few extra steps for network isolation and KMS proxy. The runtime can run in your k8s clusters or bare-metal. Note: some ops like auto-update require a control-plane link unless you take the fully air-gapped delivery.
[02:33] Ellen: ok jumping into the demo slides — Slides: https://app.redwood.ai/decks/lyonedge-demo

[03:10] Rajat (screen): first, simple schema example — a purchase-order response contract: order_id: string, items: [ { sku: string, qty: integer } ], total: number. We show how the model is constrained to emit only the JSON shape. If it deviates we have three policies: fail, repair (best-effort), or call a sanitizer function.
[03:45] Tom: show the failure mode — i want to see the sanitizer calling an internal pricing API
[03:55] Rajat: sure — here's a pre-bound function called check_pricing(url, sku_list) — you can register functions in the console with an allowed surface. In this demo i call a stubbed pricing API and the model will route to that function instead of hallucinating a price.
[04:22] Rajat: (typing) triggering the tool call — right now the transcript shows a small lag — oh there was some cross-talk —
[04:35] Speaker 2: mm-hmm
[04:36] Rajat: OK result — the function returned a canonical price object, we merge into the JSON response. The console shows the trace of calls, the model decisions, and the function payloads.
[05:00] Aisha: is that trace accessible via API for each token or just per-request? we need token-level tracing for debugging cost regressions
[05:12] Rajat: we store per-request traces including per-call latencies and token counts. Token-level breakdown is available via the console or the export API. There's a retention policy you can configure.
[05:36] Marcus: about fallbacks — say the pricing function times out, what happens?
[05:44] Rajat: we have fallback policies. You can configure model variant fallback (auto route to smaller variant), function fallback (call cached response or a synthetic response), or fail closed. There's also an automatic canary rule for new deployments that will route N% traffic and auto-roll back on error threshold.
[06:10] Priya: audit wise, do we get signed evidence of function execution? we can't just have opaque logs
[06:22] Ellen: yes, we can sign log bundles using your KMS; that's part of the enterprise pack. Also SSO and RBAC tie into console controls.
[06:40] Rajat: demo part two: live run -> a multi-step workflow: 1) model proposes a customer contact update, 2) verifies against CRM via function call, 3) writes back. We'll simulate a failure in stage 2 so you see the fallback to manual review.
[07:05] Tom: when you bind the function to CRM, how granular is the permission? we need least privilege for the function connector
[07:18] Rajat: connectors are scoped with roles; the console allows generating service principals tied to a single connector and you can scope keys to only POST to select endpoints.
[07:36] Aisha: quick ask — can we pin schema version per route? i.e., versioned contracts for rolling changes
[07:46] Rajat: absolutely. You can pin schema id and model version together; we support rollouts where new schema versions can be canaried and you can configure a compatibility checker against historical prompts.
[08:05] Ellen: also note Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization/profile changes and batching thresholds based on the workload you feed during the pilot. That reduces cost without changing the contract semantics.
[08:22] Devon: what's the expected throughput for a 4-gpu dedicated pool? our peak is around 250 qps for short prompts
[08:33] Rajat: depends on model; with a gpt-like 7B FP16-like variant you could get ~400-600 rps on a 4-GPU pool with continuous batching. But if you need low-latency p99 below 100ms you'd configure smaller batches with higher cost. We'll run a bench with your sample to target p99.
[09:01] Tom: how does KV caching interact with function calls and schema enforcement? will cached prefixes accidentally bypass checks?
[09:14] Rajat: good one — our KV cache stores prefix KV but schema enforcement runs on the final output stage; cached tokens are still validated and sanitizer functions run if mismatch detected. We can also pin caching policy per route. Sometimes transcripts say K-V cash, which i love.
[09:40] Priya: anything we should be aware of for data residency? we need EU-only for a subset of workloads
[09:49] Ellen: we can route traffic by policy and region; hosted EU regions or a Private VPC in your region. For EU-only you can do Private with dedicated control plane in region.
[10:05] Rajat: moving to the console — show the schema editor, function binding UI, and the runtime logs. (screen) The console shows the contract violations in red, and offers one-click repair or create a sanitizer.
[10:35] Aisha: is there a way to automate repairs with a human-in-the-loop queue? we don't want silent repairs in some cases
[10:46] Rajat: yes, you can route repairs to a manual review queue via webhooks or to your ticketing system, or set a policy to always require manual approval for certain keys.
[11:10] Tom: about pricing — is function calls metered separately? we need to understand unit economics for a high-call-rate workflow
[11:20] Ellen: function calls are currently charged as part of the request evaluation units and outbound connector usage; we'll send a detailed pricing sheet. For analysis we can estimate cost per request given token counts and call frequency.
[11:38] Devon: can we run a short pilot that only exercises the tool calling path, not full production?
[11:46] Ellen: yes — typical pilot is 2-4 weeks, dedicated 2-GPU pool, schema-backed routes, and specific SLAs. We'll include rollback runbooks.
[12:05] Rajat: technical deep-dive: show fallback simulation. I'm going to throttle the pricing function and show canary rollback when error exceeds threshold.
[12:22] (demo runs, simulated errors)
[13:00] Speaker 2: hmm
[13:04] Rajat: you can see the routing rule kicked in and traffic shifted to fallback model, console shows a timeline and the rollback action with reason code.
[13:30] Marcus: how are alerts emitted? we want to plug into PagerDuty and slack
[13:41] Rajat: alerts via webhook, PagerDuty integration, and we emit structured events to your event bus. You can filter alerts by route, model, or error class.
[13:55] Priya: encryption question — we want all function payloads encrypted in transit and at rest, and we may need HSM-backed signing for audit bundles
[14:08] Ellen: supported — we integrate with external KMS/HSM; we can sign bundles on your key and include verifiable signatures in the exported artifacts. We'll follow up with details and the HSM integration doc.
[14:30] Aisha: ok, last product question — if we start with hosted and then later move to private, how much rework?
[14:42] Rajat: the API surface is identical; the main differences are network and credential plumbing. Workflows, schema IDs, and contract bindings move with minimal changes. We recommend exporting your route configs and importing into the private control plane; we'll provide migration tools.
[15:05] Ellen: quick recap and pilot proposal — 2-week pilot, 2-GPU dedicated pool, schema-backed endpoints for the CRM and pricing flow, run a KV cache bench, SRE-focused canary and rollback tests, security review in parallel.
[15:26] Aisha: that sounds reasonable. any blockers?
[15:30] Priya: need to get legal + security signoff on data flows; also we need an NDA amendment for the on-prem bits
[15:38] Ellen: we'll route that to legal — i'll include the standard amendment and list of artifacts.
[15:46] Jonas: i'll coordinate the tech kickoff and send a calendar invite for the POC kickoff week of 2027-10-18
[15:52] Devon: also share the sample workload format so we can prepare data
[16:00] Ellen: noted. we'll follow up with SOW, pricing, and the benchmark script.
[16:10] (wrap-up)
[16:20] Tom: thanks all, this was helpful
[16:25] Aisha: thanks everyone
[16:30] Ellen: thanks, we'll follow up via email with links and next steps — end
